title: Simple interest

objectives.text: Calculate simple interest on a principal amount for a given rate and time.
Explain why the interest rate must be annualised before comparing offers.
Recognise that simple interest is a teaching model, while many loans work differently.

explanation: Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount, called the principal. The formula is interest equals principal times rate times time, divided by 100. Borrow ₹100 at 10% simple interest for one year and you repay ₹100 plus ₹10, which is ₹110.

The rate must always be annualised. RBI's FAME material warns that a lender may advertise 2% while the small print says per month, which works out to 24% a year. Converting every offer to a yearly rate is the only fair way to compare a loan, a deposit or a credit card.

Simple interest is a clean way to learn the idea, but most bank and NBFC loans do not use it. They typically charge interest on a reducing balance, so the effective cost differs from the simple-interest figure. Always read the sanction letter and ask for the annualised rate and the total repayment.

examples.title: One year at 10%
examples.text: Ravi borrows ₹100 for one year at 10% simple interest. Interest is 100 × 10 × 1 ÷ 100 = ₹10, so he repays ₹110 in total.

examples.title: The monthly rate trap
examples.text: A shop advertises a loan at 'just 2%'. The small print says 2% per month. Annualised, that is about 24% a year, which is very different from 2%.

keyTakeaways: Simple interest is charged only on the original principal.
Always convert a quoted rate to a yearly rate before comparing.
Most bank loans use reducing-balance interest, not simple interest.

review.notes: The ₹100 at 10% example, the formula and the monthly-rate warning are checked against RBI FAME 4th edition, Message 6. Awaiting a named human reviewer.

quiz.question: You borrow ₹1,000 at 10% simple interest for two years. How much interest do you pay?
quiz.explanation: Simple interest is charged on the original principal only: 1,000 × 10 × 2 ÷ 100 = ₹200.

quiz.question: A lender quotes '2% per month'. What is the annualised rate?
quiz.explanation: RBI's FAME material uses exactly this example: 2% per month works out to about 24% per year.

quiz.question: Why should you not assume a bank loan costs the simple-interest figure you calculated?
options: Because bank loans usually charge interest on a reducing balance
Because banks do not charge interest
Because simple interest applies only to deposits
quiz.explanation: Most bank and NBFC loans use reducing-balance interest, so the total cost differs from a simple-interest calculation on the full principal.

disclaimer: General financial education, not personalised advice. Loan terms, fees and effective rates vary by lender; read the sanction letter.
